adrs.title: LangGraph as ROOT Harness orchestration engine
adrs.context: SAGE provides the state substrate for AI-assisted workflows but deliberately excludes orchestration concerns: agent dispatch, workflow sequencing, policy enforcement, and gatekeeper coordination. ROOT Harness requires an orchestration layer above SAGE to manage multi-agent execution. SAGE's open design question regarding agent orchestration framework selection required resolution before the ROOT Harness architecture could be specified.

options_considered.option: LangGraph
options_considered.summary: Graph-based stateful orchestration framework by LangChain. Nodes as agents, edges as control flow, built-in checkpointing, human-in-the-loop interrupts, LangSmith observability. MIT-licensed, Python-native, production-standard as of 2026.
pros: Graph-based state machines map naturally to pipeline stage transitions and conditional branching
Built-in checkpointing provides durable execution for long-running workflows
Human-in-the-loop interrupt nodes implement overseer approval gates
LangSmith observability is the best available for debugging agent failures
Market leader: VP of Engineering hire most likely to have production experience with it
Transport abstractions support SAGE's phased deployment model (stdio to HTTP)
cons: Framework dependency adds coupling
LangChain ecosystem can be opinionated about abstractions

options_considered.option: CrewAI
options_considered.summary: Role-based multi-agent framework. Agents defined by role, backstory, and goal, organized into crews with sequential or hierarchical processes.
pros: Role-based model maps intuitively to gatekeeper agents
Fast prototyping, lowest learning curve
Growing adoption for business workflow automation
cons: Opinionated pipeline model assumes the framework owns state; conflicts with SAGE as state authority
Sequential/hierarchical process model does not cleanly express precondition-gate patterns
Would require duplicating state management or bending the framework

options_considered.option: AutoGen
options_considered.summary: Microsoft Research framework for conversational multi-agent collaboration. Agents interact through chat-like exchanges.
pros: Strong for exploratory, open-ended tasks
Good for research and creative problem-solving
cons: Conversational model is unpredictable for deterministic, policy-driven workflows
State management across 10+ agents is problematic
Microsoft has shifted to maintenance mode in favor of broader Agent Framework

options_considered.option: Custom thin layer
options_considered.summary: Python asyncio with simple finite state machines and direct SAGE Core API calls. Estimated 500-1000 lines of purpose-built code.
pros: Zero framework overhead or coupling
Exactly fits the need with no unused abstractions
Full control over every architectural decision
cons: Must build checkpointing, retry logic, and interrupt handling from scratch
Risk of accidental complexity as requirements grow
Would eventually reimplement LangGraph primitives (agent delegation, parallel execution with merge, conditional retry)

adrs.decision: Use LangGraph as the orchestration engine for ROOT Harness.
adrs.rationale: LangGraph provides the three capabilities most critical to ROOT Harness that would be expensive to build from scratch: durable checkpointed execution, human-in-the-loop interrupts, and production-grade observability via LangSmith. Its graph-based model aligns with SAGE's own architectural vocabulary. The dark factory development model demands failure-recoverable agent execution, which is LangGraph's core competency. CrewAI and AutoGen were eliminated on architectural fit. The custom approach was viable but risks accumulating undifferentiated complexity.
consequences: The boundary rule is established: LangGraph nodes call SAGE Core API for all state queries and mutations. LangGraph manages execution flow, checkpointing, and human interrupts. SAGE manages document state, lifecycle, authority, and governance. LangGraph never maintains a parallel copy of document state.
ROOT Harness inherits a Python runtime dependency and LangChain ecosystem coupling.
Agent definitions must be expressible as LangGraph node/edge configurations.
LangSmith becomes the observability layer for agent execution debugging.
SAGE's open design question regarding agent orchestration framework selection is resolved.

adrs.title: Separation of SAGE, ROOT Harness, and domain instantiation documents
adrs.context: The SAGE Architecture Reference v0.3.3 contained a PIM Health Instantiation appendix (Appendix A) with domain-specific configuration, agent definitions, pipeline stages, and team structure. Three concerns converged requiring separation: (1) the LangGraph decision (ADR-001) creates new orchestration content that is partly general and partly PIM-specific; (2) SAGE should be shareable without disclosing PIM details, including patent codes, filing pipeline, gatekeeper agents, and attorney relationships; (3) ROOT Harness is Clif's personal agentic ecosystem experiment serving multiple domains, not a PIM product.

options_considered.option: PIM-centric document with SAGE as a component
options_considered.summary: Create a new PIM-specific document that absorbs orchestration architecture, agent definitions, and SAGE integration details. PIM is the organizing principle; SAGE and LangGraph are described as components serving PIM.
pros: PIM is the most complex and well-documented use case; organizing around it provides immediate concrete content
cons: Misrepresents the system's purpose: ROOT Harness exists for transferable learning across domains, not to serve PIM
Embeds a single use case as the structural assumption, making future domains feel like afterthoughts
Conflates the experiment (building an agentic ecosystem) with one of its test cases (PIM)

options_considered.option: Split PIM content into a standalone PIM document; SAGE remains general-purpose
options_considered.summary: Remove Appendix A from SAGE. Create a new PIM-specific document for all domain content. No ecosystem-level document.
pros: SAGE becomes shareable without PIM disclosure
Clean separation of infrastructure from domain
cons: No home for domain-neutral orchestration architecture, agent patterns, or development environment documentation
Frames the new document as PIM-specific when the real scope is broader
Loses the experimental/learning framing that gives the work its durable value

options_considered.option: Three-layer separation: SAGE (memory), ROOT Harness (ecosystem), domain instantiations (appendices)
options_considered.summary: SAGE Architecture Reference describes the memory system (general-purpose, shareable). ROOT Harness Architecture Reference describes the orchestration ecosystem (general-purpose body, domain appendices). PIM Health Instantiation lives as Appendix A of the ROOT Harness document.
pros: Correctly scopes ROOT Harness as Clif's personal experiment, not a PIM product
SAGE is shareable independently
ROOT Harness body (Sections 1-8) is shareable independently
PIM content is isolated in an appendix that can be withheld
Architecture supports future domain instantiations (Resurrection, college basketball, personal) without structural changes
Document structure mirrors the system's actual purpose: transferable learning across domains
cons: Three documents to maintain instead of one

adrs.decision: Adopt the three-layer separation. SAGE Architecture Reference describes the memory system. ROOT Harness Architecture Reference describes the orchestration ecosystem. PIM Health Instantiation lives as Appendix A of the ROOT Harness document.
adrs.rationale: The document structure should reflect the system's actual purpose. ROOT Harness exists to gain transferable learning across domains through disciplined experimentation. Organizing the documentation the same way ensures general patterns are clearly separated from domain-specific configuration. The shareability requirement is met at two levels: SAGE can be shared alone, and ROOT Harness Sections 1-8 can be shared without the PIM appendix. The PIM-centric framing was rejected because it privileged one test case as the organizing principle, obscuring the experimental purpose that gives the work its durable value.
consequences: SAGE Architecture Reference becomes a domain-neutral memory system document with no PIM-specific content.
ROOT Harness Architecture Reference is created with a domain-neutral body and PIM Health Instantiation as an appendix.
Both documents use separate namespace prefixes (SAGE_ and ROOT_), not PIM_ codes.
The ADR store is established as a separate authority for cross-cutting decisions (see ADR-004).

adrs.title: ROOT Harness naming and identity
adrs.context: The agentic ecosystem needed a name distinct from SAGE (its memory component) and from any domain instantiation (PIM, Resurrection, etc.). The name needed to be domain-neutral, suggest a system of cooperating parts, and be shareable with technical peers. The naming process began with exploration of nouns and adjectives across metaphorical families, then considered combining a modifier with 'Harness' after noting the word's growing usage in AI-based software development, and finally evaluated acronym possibilities.

options_considered.option: Standalone nouns (Forge, Trellis, Loom, Reef, etc.)
options_considered.summary: Single-word names from various metaphorical families: workshop/making, structure/support, living systems, coordination, connective tissue.
pros: Simple and memorable
Several strong candidates (Forge, Trellis, Loom)
cons: No connection to the 'harness' concept that resonated with all three relevant metaphors (test harness, wiring harness, working harness)

options_considered.option: Modifier + Harness combinations
options_considered.summary: Two-word names pairing a descriptive modifier with Harness: Dark Harness, Proof Harness, Root Harness, etc.
pros: 'Harness' carries test harness, wiring harness, and working harness metaphors simultaneously
Modifier provides differentiation and personality
cons: Two-word name is slightly heavier than a single word

options_considered.option: ROOT Harness (Runtime for Orchestration, Operations, and Testing)
options_considered.summary: ROOT as a backronym where each letter earns its place: Runtime (it runs agents), Orchestration (LangGraph coordination), Operations (real-world workflow management), Testing (experimental discipline). 'Root' also carries metaphors of foundation and the root system connecting diverse surface growth.
pros: Acronym expansion maps precisely to the four design goals
Natural-language word 'root' reinforces foundational/transferable learning purpose
Pairs well with SAGE: roots and wisdom, infrastructure and memory
Domain-neutral and technically descriptive
cons: Backronyms can feel forced; this one holds up under scrutiny but should be evaluated honestly

adrs.decision: Name the agentic ecosystem ROOT Harness. ROOT expands to Runtime for Orchestration, Operations, and Testing.
adrs.rationale: The name satisfies all constraints: domain-neutral, distinct from SAGE, suggests a system of cooperating parts, and communicates immediately to a technical audience. The acronym expansion maps to the system's actual purpose without forcing any letter. The root/sage pairing creates a coherent naming vocabulary for the two core components.
consequences: ROOT Harness uses the ROOT_ namespace prefix.
SAGE retains independent identity and its own namespace; it is ROOT Harness's memory component but not subordinate to it.
Domain instantiations are consumers of ROOT Harness, referred to as ROOT Harness instantiations.
The harness.io naming collision is noted but accepted as low-risk for a personal experimental system.

adrs.title: ADR methodology: JSON store as separate authority
adrs.context: Architecture decisions for ROOT Harness and SAGE cross document boundaries: the LangGraph decision affects ROOT Harness, SAGE, and PIM simultaneously. Embedding ADRs as appendices in their primary document creates either a scoping problem (where does a cross-cutting ADR go?) or duplication (violating single-authority). A separate ADR authority was needed. The format needed to be both human-reviewable and agent-consumable, since ROOT Harness agents will be first-class ADR consumers.

options_considered.option: ADRs as full appendices in their primary document
options_considered.summary: Each ADR lives as a complete appendix in the document it most directly affects. Cross-cutting ADRs are placed in one document and cross-referenced from others.
pros: Self-contained: each document carries its own decision history
No additional files to manage
cons: Cross-cutting ADRs have no natural home; cross-references create staleness risk
Violates source authority principle: the ADR content would exist in one document but be referenced from others, creating ambiguous authority when documents diverge
Not agent-friendly: decisions are embedded in Word document prose

options_considered.option: Markdown files in a local directory
options_considered.summary: One .md file per ADR in ~/adr/, using a structured Markdown template. SAGE ingests the directory when it comes online.
pros: Human-readable in any text editor
SAGE's Markdown adapter handles ingestion natively
Git diffs are legible per-ADR
cons: Not natively queryable without parsing Markdown headers
Less agent-friendly than structured data
Multiple files to manage

options_considered.option: Single JSON file as ADR store
options_considered.summary: One JSON file containing an array of ADR objects with a defined schema. Documents carry an ADR index appendix (table of pointers) rather than full ADR content.
pros: Natively queryable: filter by status, scope, tags, affected documents, date range
Agent-friendly: structured data consumed directly by ROOT Harness agents
Atomic: one file to back up, version-control, and eventually ingest into SAGE
Schema-enforceable: ADR structure can be validated programmatically
cons: SAGE's Phase 1 has no JSON adapter; ingestion requires a custom adapter or preprocessing step
Less human-readable than Markdown without rendering tooling
Git diffs on a single file are noisier than per-ADR file diffs

adrs.decision: Use a single JSON file as the ADR store, maintained as a separate source authority. Documents carry an ADR index appendix (a table listing ADR number, title, date, and status for ADRs affecting that document). Revision history entries reference ADR numbers instead of embedding decision rationale. The single-file structure will be revisited if the store grows unwieldy.
adrs.rationale: The ADR store's primary consumers are agents, not humans. JSON is the natural format for agent consumption. Human readability is solved by rendering, not by storage format. The single-file approach is the simplest structure that supports programmatic querying. The SAGE ingestion gap is acceptable because writing a JSON-to-projection adapter is trivial and fits SAGE's adapter architecture. Establishing ADRs as a separate authority avoids the cross-document scoping problem and respects the source authority principle.
consequences: The ADR store is maintained as a single JSON file at a known local path, independent of any document namespace.
Architecture documents carry an ADR Index appendix with pointers (ADR number, title, date, status), not full ADR content.
Architecture document revision histories reference ADR numbers for traceability without redundancy.
A JSON source adapter for SAGE becomes a low-priority backlog item for eventual ingestion of the ADR store.
Schema version is tracked in the store file to support future schema evolution.

adrs.title: PIM Health Instantiation as independent document
adrs.context: ADR-002 placed PIM Health Instantiation as Appendix A of the ROOT Harness Architecture Reference, with the appendix withholdable for shareability. In practice, this left ROOT Harness carrying domain-specific content in its structure. Promoting PIM to a fully independent document achieves a stronger separation: ROOT Harness has zero withholdable content, and PIM documentation can evolve on its own cadence without triggering ROOT Harness revisions.

options_considered.option: Retain PIM as ROOT Harness Appendix A (status quo per ADR-002)
options_considered.summary: Keep the three-layer model: SAGE (memory), ROOT Harness body (orchestration), PIM appendix (withholdable).
pros: Already decided and documented
Fewer documents to maintain
cons: ROOT Harness still carries withholdable content, complicating sharing
PIM changes trigger ROOT Harness revision history updates
Appendix coupling grows as PIM documentation matures

options_considered.option: PIM Health Instance as a fully independent document
options_considered.summary: PIM documentation stands alone, referencing SAGE and ROOT Harness by document name. ROOT Harness body and appendices contain no domain-specific content.
pros: ROOT Harness is fully shareable with no withheld sections
PIM documentation evolves independently with its own revision cadence
Clean model for future domain instantiations: each is its own document
ROOT Harness describes the instantiation model generically; instances demonstrate it
cons: One more document to maintain
Cross-references between PIM and ROOT Harness require manual consistency

adrs.decision: PIM Health Instantiation becomes a fully independent document. ROOT Harness describes the domain instantiation model generically but carries no domain-specific content. This supersedes ADR-002's appendix placement.
adrs.rationale: The stronger separation eliminates the last shareability constraint on ROOT Harness and correctly models the relationship between the ecosystem and its use cases. Each domain instantiation is a consumer of ROOT Harness and SAGE, not a component of either. The additional maintenance cost of a separate document is outweighed by the cleaner separation of concerns and independent revision cadence.
consequences: ADR-002 status changes to superseded.
ROOT Harness carries no domain-specific content. Its domain instantiation model describes the pattern generically.
PIM Health Instance is created as a standalone deliverable referencing SAGE and ROOT Harness.
Future domain instantiations (Resurrection, college basketball, personal) follow the same independent-document pattern.

adrs.title: Deployment model separation from ROOT Harness
adrs.context: The ROOT Harness outline draft included a Section 7 (Development Environment) covering Mac Mini hardware, SAGE Phase 1, LangGraph local setup, and production mapping. This content mixes architectural constraints (what the system requires at each deployment phase) with operational details (specific hardware, tool versions, local paths, setup procedures). These change at different cadences and serve different readers.

options_considered.option: Keep all deployment and environment content in ROOT Harness Section 7
options_considered.summary: A single section covers both the architectural deployment model and concrete environment details.
pros: Self-contained: everything about running the system is in one place
Fewer documents
cons: Tool version bumps and hardware changes trigger architecture document revisions
Mixes content that serves different readers (system designers vs. operators)
Architecture document accumulates operational drift

options_considered.option: Thin deployment model section in ROOT Harness; concrete environment details in a separate operational artifact
options_considered.summary: ROOT Harness retains an architectural deployment model section (analogous to SAGE Section 3.2) describing requirements and phasing. A separate Deployment Model document captures current hardware, installed tools, local paths, and setup procedures.
pros: Architecture document stays stable; operational details change independently
Serves different readers appropriately
Parallels SAGE's own deployment model section structure
Operational artifact can include setup procedures and troubleshooting that would be out of place in an architecture reference
cons: One more document in the ecosystem

adrs.decision: ROOT Harness retains a thin Deployment Model section describing architectural requirements and phasing. Concrete environment details (hardware, tool versions, paths, setup procedures) move to a separate Deployment Model document.
adrs.rationale: Architecture documents should describe constraints that are expensive to reverse. Hardware specs, tool versions, and local paths are cheap to change and change frequently. Separating them prevents operational churn from polluting the architecture revision history. The parallel with SAGE Section 3.2 provides a consistent structural pattern across the CAS document portfolio.
consequences: ROOT Harness retains an architectural deployment model section scoped to requirements and phase descriptions.
A separate Deployment Model document is created as an operational artifact in the CAS ecosystem.
Setup procedures, hardware specifications, and tool version inventories live exclusively in the Deployment Model document.

adrs.title: CAS: Clif's Agentic System as portfolio umbrella name
adrs.context: ROOT Harness was serving double duty as both the orchestration layer name and the informal identity for the entire ecosystem. When discussing the full set of deliverables (architecture documents, formal specs, test plans, code, domain instantiations), there was no name for the portfolio as a whole. This created ambiguity about whether ROOT Harness referred to the orchestration component or the entire system.

options_considered.option: Use ROOT Harness as the umbrella name
options_considered.summary: Continue using ROOT Harness to refer to both the orchestration layer and the ecosystem as a whole, relying on context to disambiguate.
pros: No new name to introduce
Already established in ADR-003
cons: Ambiguous: 'ROOT Harness' sometimes means the orchestration component, sometimes the whole system
Confusion worsens as the ecosystem grows beyond SAGE and ROOT Harness

options_considered.option: CAS (Clif's Agentic System)
options_considered.summary: A portfolio-level name that encompasses SAGE, ROOT Harness, domain instantiations, the ADR store, formal specs, test plans, and working code.
pros: Resolves the ambiguity: CAS is the ecosystem, ROOT Harness is the orchestration component, SAGE is the memory system
Personal and honest: this is Clif's experimental system, not a product
Lightweight enough to use in conversation without ceremony
cons: Introduces a third name to track alongside SAGE and ROOT Harness
Not an acronym with a natural-language resonance the way ROOT and SAGE are

adrs.decision: Adopt CAS (Clif's Agentic System) as the umbrella name for the entire portfolio. SAGE and ROOT Harness retain their existing identities as components within CAS.
adrs.rationale: The naming ambiguity was already causing confusion in conversation. A portfolio-level name that is clearly distinct from its components eliminates the problem. The personal framing ('Clif's') is appropriate because this is an experimental system for transferable learning, not a product. CAS is simple, unambiguous, and carries no metaphorical weight that might conflict with SAGE or ROOT.
consequences: CAS is the portfolio-level name. SAGE and ROOT Harness are components within it.
ROOT Harness is unambiguously the orchestration component, not the ecosystem name.
SAGE is unambiguously the memory component.
Future artifacts (formal specs, test plans, code repositories) are organized under the CAS umbrella.

adrs.title: Formal substrate as independent CAS artifact
adrs.context: The formal substrate concept -- specification-level content extracted from architecture documents into executable form (API contracts, schemas, state machines, validators) -- was discussed in the prior session but never scoped to a home. Three placement options existed: a section within ROOT Harness, a section within SAGE, or a separate artifact. The substrate spans both SAGE and ROOT Harness: SAGE contributes Core API contracts, object model schemas, lifecycle state machine definitions, edge type taxonomy validators, and vault configuration schemas. ROOT Harness contributes orchestration API contracts, agent registration schemas, pipeline configuration schemas, and human-in-the-loop interrupt contracts. Domain instantiations contribute pipeline stage definitions, policy maps, and gatekeeper configurations. Additionally, ROOT Harness is expected to expose its own REST API and MCP servers for orchestration operations (human-in-the-loop approvals, pipeline status, workflow triggers), making the ROOT Harness formal substrate a practical near-term need, not a theoretical concern.

options_considered.option: Section within ROOT Harness Architecture Reference
options_considered.summary: A formal substrate section in ROOT Harness describes and embeds the executable specifications for both ROOT Harness and SAGE.
pros: Self-contained within the orchestration document
cons: SAGE specifications don't belong in a ROOT Harness document
Violates the separation that keeps SAGE independently shareable
Architecture documents should describe what gets specified and why, not contain the specifications themselves

options_considered.option: Split across both architecture documents
options_considered.summary: SAGE Architecture Reference contains SAGE specifications; ROOT Harness contains ROOT Harness specifications.
pros: Each document owns its own specifications
No new document needed
cons: Specifications change at a different cadence than architecture prose
Domain-specific substrate (PIM pipeline definitions, policy maps) has no home
No unified location for cross-cutting contracts (e.g., the interface between ROOT Harness and SAGE)

options_considered.option: Formal substrate as an independent CAS artifact
options_considered.summary: A separate deliverable containing all executable specifications across the CAS portfolio. Architecture documents describe what gets specified and why; the formal substrate artifact contains the specifications themselves. Organized by component (SAGE, ROOT Harness) with domain-specific sections added per instantiation.
pros: Single source authority for all executable specifications
Changes at its own cadence without triggering architecture document revisions
Cross-cutting contracts (SAGE-ROOT Harness interface) have a natural home
Domain instantiation substrate (PIM pipeline definitions) extends the same artifact
Parallels the ADR store pattern: a separate authority referenced by pointer from architecture documents
cons: One more artifact in the ecosystem
Requires clear cross-referencing discipline between architecture documents and the substrate

adrs.decision: Formal substrate is an independent CAS artifact. Architecture documents describe what gets specified formally and why. The formal substrate artifact contains the actual executable specifications (OpenAPI contracts, Pydantic/JSON Schema models, state machine definitions, validators, configuration schemas), organized by component.
adrs.rationale: The formal substrate spans SAGE, ROOT Harness, and domain instantiations. No single architecture document is the right home for cross-cutting specifications. The substrate changes at a different cadence than architecture prose -- schemas evolve during implementation while architecture remains stable. The pattern mirrors the ADR store: a separate source authority referenced by pointer from the documents it serves. ROOT Harness's anticipated REST API and MCP servers make the orchestration substrate a practical near-term need alongside SAGE's existing Core API contracts.
consequences: The Formal Substrate is an independent artifact in the CAS portfolio.
The substrate is organized by component (SAGE, ROOT Harness) with domain-specific sections added per instantiation.
The formal substrate becomes a primary input to the test plan: each formal specification becomes a testable assertion.
The formal substrate is a candidate for eventual SAGE ingestion alongside the ADR store.

adrs.title: CAS Overview as independent portfolio document
adrs.context: Portfolio-level content -- CAS identity, the four goals, five design principles, component relationships, and document navigation -- was assigned to ROOT Harness Section 1 and Section 2 by default because ROOT Harness was the next document to be written. However, ROOT Harness is a component, not the portfolio. Assigning portfolio identity to a component document creates a concern leak: a reader must start with the 'right' component document to understand the ecosystem, and the component document carries weight above its station.

options_considered.option: Keep portfolio content in ROOT Harness Sections 1 and 2
options_considered.summary: ROOT Harness introduction bootstraps CAS context for the reader, then narrows to orchestration concerns.
pros: No additional document
Already planned in ROOT Harness outline v2.1
cons: ROOT Harness Section 1 does double duty: portfolio identity and component introduction
Design goals in Section 2 are portfolio-level, not component-level
A reader who starts with SAGE has no portfolio context
Component document carries portfolio authority it should not own

options_considered.option: Create a CAS Overview as an independent portfolio document
options_considered.summary: A thin document that owns portfolio identity, goals, design principles, component descriptions, ecosystem artifact inventory, and a document reading guide. ROOT Harness drops its design goals section and narrows Section 1 to component scope with a pointer to the overview.
pros: Portfolio identity has a proper home with clear source authority
ROOT Harness Section 1 narrows to its actual scope
Any reader can start with the overview regardless of which component they care about
Parallels the pattern of separating concerns into independent documents (ADR-005, ADR-006, ADR-008)
Stabilizes early and changes rarely
cons: One more document in the ecosystem

adrs.decision: Create a CAS Overview as an independent portfolio document. It owns CAS identity, the four goals, the five design principles, component descriptions, ecosystem artifact inventory, and the document reading guide. ROOT Harness narrows to component identity and scope with a pointer to the CAS Overview.
adrs.rationale: The Source Authority Rule requires that content belong to exactly one authority. Portfolio identity, goals, and principles are cross-cutting concerns that do not belong to any component. Assigning them to ROOT Harness created a concern leak visible in the outline: Section 1 doing double duty and Section 2 carrying portfolio-level content. The CAS Overview resolves this cleanly and provides a natural entry point for any reader. The document is thin (comparable to the Deployment Model) and expected to stabilize early.
consequences: CAS Overview is added to the canonical document list as the recommended starting point.
ROOT Harness narrows to component scope; portfolio-level goals and principles belong to the CAS Overview.
Future portfolio-level concerns (e.g., cross-component naming conventions, shared design vocabulary) have a natural home in the CAS Overview.

adrs.title: Steward agent model and two-type agent taxonomy
adrs.context: ROOT Harness v0.1 defines agents with a four-value agent_type enum (autonomous, gatekeeper, mechanical, interactive) and a boundary rule stating that LangGraph nodes call SAGE Core API for all state queries and mutations. The gatekeeper pattern is defined as a specialized agent that guards transitions between pipeline stages. This model has three architectural weaknesses. First, any agent can call SAGE directly, meaning artifact ownership is implicit rather than enforced. Second, the gatekeeper is defined as a standalone agent type, but its four responsibilities (precondition evaluation, evidence assembly, decision routing, transition execution) are inherent to any agent that governs write access to a canonical artifact. Third, orchestrator agents and artifact-owning agents are not structurally distinguished, creating ambiguity about which agent is responsible for coordination versus artifact integrity. Analysis of the PIM Health domain (glossary changes propagating to patent documents) and software development domains (bounded code modules with exclusive ownership) revealed a consistent pattern: canonical artifacts benefit from a dedicated agent that owns all access, mediates both reads and writes, and enforces domain rules on mutations. This pattern generalizes from REST API design, where a resource endpoint owns its noun and exposes a uniform verb interface.

options_considered.option: Retain v0.1 agent taxonomy with refinements
options_considered.summary: Keep the four-value agent_type enum and the standalone gatekeeper pattern. Add artifact ownership as an optional annotation on agent registration records.
pros: No structural change to the existing architecture
Minimal revision to ROOT Harness v0.1
cons: Artifact ownership remains optional rather than architecturally enforced
Gatekeeper remains a separate agent type when its behavior is intrinsic to artifact ownership
Any agent can still call SAGE directly, leaving the orchestrator unable to reason about the full execution graph
Does not address the context-efficiency problem: orchestrators still load full artifacts for targeted queries

options_considered.option: Steward agent model with two-type taxonomy
options_considered.summary: Each canonical artifact gets a dedicated agent (a steward) that owns all read and write access. Orchestrators coordinate stewards but never access artifacts directly. Tools are stateless capabilities, not agents. Two-type taxonomy: stewards own canonical artifacts; orchestrators own coordination lifecycles.
pros: Single-writer guarantee per artifact
Context-efficient retrieval: orchestrators get targeted answers without loading full artifacts
Uniform interface: orchestrators interact with any artifact through the same verb vocabulary
Gatekeeper behavior absorbed naturally into the artifact owner's write path
Clean generalization from REST API resource-endpoint design
Self-documenting naming convention: 'glossary_steward' communicates role immediately
cons: New terminology to introduce to the architectural vocabulary
Every canonical artifact requires a dedicated agent, increasing the agent roster

adrs.decision: Adopt the steward agent model with a two-type agent taxonomy. A steward is the sole authority over a canonical artifact, responsible for both enforcing write rules (including precondition evaluation, evidence assembly, and decision routing) and serving context-efficient read slices. An orchestrator owns a coordination lifecycle: it plans work (collaboratively with the human), dispatches stewards according to the plan, tracks progress, and handles failures. Tools are stateless capabilities that stewards and orchestrators invoke; they are not agents and do not appear in the agent registry. The agent_type enum becomes: steward, orchestrator. The standalone gatekeeper agent type is retired; gatekeeping is the steward's mutation-governance behavior.
adrs.rationale: The steward model enforces artifact ownership structurally rather than by convention. It resolves three problems simultaneously: (1) the gatekeeper's four responsibilities are inherent to any agent that owns a canonical artifact, eliminating the need for a standalone gatekeeper type; (2) the boundary rule becomes a two-tier statement where stewards call SAGE and orchestrators call stewards, giving the orchestrator complete visibility into the execution graph; (3) context-efficient retrieval is built into the architecture rather than left as an optimization. The two-type taxonomy (steward and orchestrator) is validated across two domains: PIM Health (glossary_steward, patent_steward, fs_steward) and software development (auth_steward, payments_service_steward), confirming generality. The REST resource-endpoint analogy provides a well-understood design precedent. Five naming candidates were evaluated for the artifact-owning agent type: 'noun' (precise but abstract, requires the REST analogy to communicate), 'gatekeeper' (overemphasizes blocking, carries v0.1 baggage), 'custodian' (emphasizes maintenance over judgment), 'trustee' (emphasizes obligation over competence), and 'steward' (naturally covers access mediation, mutation governance, and delegated authority). 'Steward' was selected because it self-documents all three responsibilities without overemphasizing any one and scales naturally as a naming convention across domains.
consequences: The boundary rule becomes a two-tier statement: steward agents call SAGE Core API for operations on their owned artifacts; orchestrator agents access artifacts exclusively through the owning steward; orchestrators access SAGE directly only for their own transient working state.

The agent taxonomy reduces to two types: steward (owns a canonical artifact) and orchestrator (owns a coordination lifecycle). The v0.1 four-value enum and the standalone gatekeeper agent type are retired.
Agent registration records gain an owned_artifact field, making artifact ownership explicit and queryable.

Gatekeeping is absorbed into the steward contract as mutation governance: precondition evaluation, evidence assembly, decision routing, and transition execution are the steward's write-path behavior, not a separate agent role.
The vault_steward mediates cross-artifact infrastructure queries (semantic search, blast radius analysis, graph traversals), ensuring orchestrators never call SAGE directly for discovery operations.
The no-peer-calls rule is the default architectural stance: stewards do not call peer stewards; all inter-artifact coordination routes through orchestrators.
The CAS Overview gains two portfolio-level design principles: steward-mediated access and orchestrator-mediated coordination.
Domain instantiation documents define which stewards the domain needs and their domain-specific configurations.
The formal substrate gains an updated agent registration schema reflecting the two-type taxonomy.

adrs.title: Semantic abstract generation at ingestion
adrs.context: SAGE's ingestion pipeline produces indexable projections (faithful structural renderings of source documents) that are chunked by heading hierarchy and embedded for retrieval. This pipeline is effective for locating specific content within documents but provides no mechanism for document-level semantic orientation: understanding what a document is about, why it matters, and how it relates to query intent before diving into chunk-level results. An external article (Zak El Fassi, 'How Do You Want to Remember?', March 2026) documented a pattern where a memory system achieved perfect recall of events and temporal sequences but only 25% recall on decision rationale. The fix was structural: co-locating the 'why' with the 'what' so retrieval could find both. The same gap exists in SAGE: raw projections of verbose source types (session transcripts, meeting notes, correspondence) carry low semantic density per chunk, while terse source types (patent claims, formal specifications) carry high density that benefits from explication. Both cases produce retrieval failures when users search for document-level meaning rather than specific content.

options_considered.option: Enhance the projection itself to be semantically dense
options_considered.summary: Modify source adapters to produce projections that compress or explicate source content rather than faithfully rendering it.
pros: No new field on the document record
No additional pipeline stage
cons: Conflates two concerns: the projection serves structural fidelity (for chunking) and semantic density (for orientation) simultaneously
Loses the faithful rendering that makes projections useful for deterministic retrieval and re-chunking
Different source types need opposite treatments (compression vs. explication), making a single projection serve contradictory goals

options_considered.option: Fixed-length abstract generated at ingestion
options_considered.summary: Add a semantic_abstract field to the document record, generated by an LLM at ingestion time with a fixed maximum length (e.g., 500 tokens).
pros: Simple implementation with a single token budget
No density calculation required
cons: Produces the same distortion El Fassi identified: a fixed ceiling either truncates dense material or wastes tokens on sparse material
A 40,000-word patent document and a 2-page checklist receive the same abstract length, which serves neither well

options_considered.option: Density-proportional abstract generated at ingestion
options_considered.summary: Add a semantic_abstract field generated by an LLM with a target length calculated from source word count, structural complexity, and semantic variance across chunks. The abstract length is proportional to the information content of the source, not its word count.
pros: Normalizes semantic density across source types: verbose sources get compressed, terse sources get explicated
Proportional length ensures abstracts are useful for both large complex documents and small focused ones
Preserves the projection's role as a faithful structural rendering while adding a separate semantic orientation layer
Enables two-pass retrieval: abstract-level relevance filtering before chunk-level content extraction
Provides stewards with a pre-built, context-efficient summary for orientation queries
Density calculation uses data already produced by the chunking and embedding stage (chunk count, embedding vectors)
cons: Introduces a generative LLM dependency into the ingestion pipeline, which is currently LLM-free
Adds a third pipeline stage (projection, indexing, abstraction) with associated latency and cost
Density formula requires domain tuning via vault configuration

adrs.decision: Add a semantic_abstract field to the document record, generated by a local LLM at ingestion time with a target length proportional to the document's information density. The ingestion pipeline extends from two stages (projection, indexing) to three stages (projection, indexing, abstraction). The density calculation uses source token count, structural complexity (heading depth, section count from the projection), and semantic variance (average pairwise distance between chunk embeddings from the indexing stage). The density formula is vault-configurable to accommodate domain-specific density profiles. Abstract generation is vault-configurable (opt-in) and degrades gracefully: if the LLM is unavailable, ingestion proceeds without the abstract and flags the document for deferred generation.
adrs.rationale: The density-proportional approach resolves the core retrieval gap (document-level semantic orientation) without compromising the projection's existing role. It addresses the specific failure mode documented by El Fassi: systems that remember 'what' but not 'why'. The abstract serves three architectural consumers: (1) semantic retrieval gains a two-pass capability where abstract search filters for relevant documents before chunk search locates specific content; (2) steward agents gain a pre-built summary for responding to orientation queries without loading full artifacts into context windows; (3) the vault_steward's discovery surface gains document-level semantic context for cross-artifact queries. The decision to generate abstracts after chunking and embedding (not before) is a deliberate sequencing choice: the density calculation requires embedding vectors that only exist after the indexing stage. This means the abstract cannot influence chunking decisions, but this is acceptable because the abstract and the projection serve different retrieval patterns. Using a local LLM (running on the development machine via MLX) preserves the local-first design principle: no API calls, no network dependency, no per-token cost for abstract generation.
consequences: The document record gains a semantic_abstract field (text, nullable) stored in the graph store alongside projection_text.

The ingestion pipeline extends to three stages: projection (source adapter), indexing (chunk and embed), and abstraction (density calculation and LLM generation). The interface boundary between indexing and abstraction is the set of chunk embeddings plus projection metadata.

A density scoring algorithm computes the abstract target length from three inputs: source token count, structural complexity, and semantic variance across chunks. The algorithm's parameters are vault-configurable.
Abstract generation is vault-configurable via an opt-in flag in the vault configuration. Vaults that do not enable it skip the abstraction stage entirely.

The ingestion pipeline gains a generative LLM dependency. This is the first LLM dependency in SAGE's pipeline (the embedding model is not generative). Graceful degradation ensures ingestion is not blocked if the LLM is unavailable.
Re-ingestion via the supersedes pathway regenerates the abstract for the new document version.
The Deployment Model gains a local LLM infrastructure section documenting the runtime (MLX), model, and configuration.
The formal substrate gains a schema for the density scoring algorithm parameters and the abstract generation configuration.

adrs.title: Decision logs as SAGE-managed steward and orchestrator companion artifacts
adrs.context: CAS records architectural decisions in the ADR store and requires rationale in document revision history entries. However, neither mechanism captures operational judgment that does not produce an artifact revision: decisions not to act (a steward evaluates a potential change and concludes no change is warranted), decisions deferred (an issue is identified but resolution depends on something outside the steward's scope or the timing is not right), and cross-artifact reasoning (an orchestrator's rationale for coordinating a multi-artifact operation in a specific sequence). This gap means that judgment acquired during workflow execution is lost between sessions. An external article (Muratcan Koylan, 'The File System Is the New Database', February 2026) documented an episodic memory pattern where decisions, failures, and reasoning were stored alongside facts, enabling agents to reference prior judgment rather than generating generic advice. The same gap exists in CAS: SAGE remembers documents and their relationships, but no artifact type captures the operational reasoning that stewards and orchestrators accumulate during execution.

options_considered.option: Parallel JSON file store outside SAGE
options_considered.summary: A single JSON file per agent, maintained as a separate source authority alongside the ADR store, referenced by pointer from architecture documents.
pros: Requires zero changes to SAGE or ROOT Harness
Mirrors the ADR store pattern
cons: Creates a second memory substrate outside SAGE, contradicting SAGE's role as the memory component
Loses SAGE's retrieval capabilities (semantic search, typed relationships, lifecycle management)
Agents must look in two places for remembered context

options_considered.option: First-class SAGE document type without steward ownership
options_considered.summary: Define a judgment_record document type in SAGE's document object model as a standalone artifact, not owned by any specific steward.
pros: Full SAGE retrieval capabilities
Cross-domain queries are straightforward
cons: No clear ownership: judgment records lack a single-writer guarantee
Disconnected from the steward that produced the judgment
Violates the steward-mediated access principle if multiple agents write to the same artifact

options_considered.option: Steward-local and orchestrator-local decision logs as SAGE-managed companion artifacts
options_considered.summary: Each steward and orchestrator may own a decision log as a SAGE-managed document. The log captures operational judgment scoped to that agent's domain. Append-only, served as context-efficient read slices, searchable through the vault_steward.
pros: Judgment is stored where it is used, owned by the agent that produced it
Single-writer guarantee maintained: the owning agent is the sole writer
Full SAGE retrieval, relationship, and lifecycle capabilities
Cross-domain queries available through the vault_steward's aggregation surface
Clean boundary with revision history: decision logs cover only gap categories (decisions not to act, deferred, cross-artifact reasoning)
cons: Cross-domain judgment queries require vault_steward aggregation rather than a single-artifact scan
Increases each agent's artifact count from one to two

adrs.decision: Stewards and orchestrators may each own a decision log as a SAGE-managed companion artifact. Steward logs capture artifact-scoped operational judgment: decisions not to act and decisions deferred. Orchestrator logs capture coordination-scoped judgment: cross-artifact reasoning, dispatch sequencing rationale, and workflow halt reasoning. Logs are append-only; revised judgments are recorded as new entries with a back-reference to the superseded entry. Domain instantiations determine which agents receive decision logs. The vault_steward provides cross-log search for pattern discovery across agents.
adrs.rationale: The companion artifact approach preserves the steward model's ownership guarantees while using SAGE as the sole memory substrate. Placing decision logs outside SAGE would create a parallel memory system that contradicts SAGE's architectural role. The clean boundary with revision history avoids source authority violations: decisions that produce artifact changes are captured in the artifact's revision history with rationale (per existing convention); decision logs cover only the three gap categories that revision history cannot represent. The append-only constraint mirrors the steward mutation governance model and prevents accidental loss of judgment history. Making decision logs optional per domain instantiation respects the domain-neutral principle: not every steward accumulates judgment worth recording.
consequences: Steward agents may own a companion decision log as a SAGE-managed document in addition to their primary canonical artifact.
Orchestrator agents may own a decision log for coordination-scoped judgment.
Decision logs are append-only. Supersession is by back-reference, not modification, paralleling ADR supersession.
Decision log entries cover three categories: decisions not to act, decisions deferred, and cross-artifact reasoning. Decisions that produce artifact changes remain in the artifact's revision history.
Domain instantiations determine which agents receive decision logs as part of the agent roster configuration.
The vault_steward's discovery surface includes cross-log search for identifying recurring judgment patterns across agents.
The formal substrate gains an entry schema for decision log records.

adrs.title: Typed event stream for agent execution observability
adrs.context: ROOT Harness defines request/response operations on the Orchestration API (trigger_workflow, get_status, approve, list_pending, get_agent_history) but has no mechanism for real-time observation of agent execution. The CAS Application requires live monitoring of orchestrator and steward activity to fulfill its role as the human-facing client for oversight and approval. The existing API supports polling (get_status) but not push-based notification. LangSmith provides trace-level observability for debugging but is a development tool, not a production interface for the CAS Application. An external open-source project (OpenHarness by Max Gfeller) demonstrated a typed event stream pattern where an agent's run() method yields typed events (text.delta, tool.start, tool.done, step.done, done) that consumers iterate over to build arbitrary UIs. The pattern cleanly separates execution from presentation and provides the real-time observability substrate that the CAS Application needs.

options_considered.option: Polling-only via existing get_status operation
options_considered.summary: The CAS Application periodically calls get_status to check workflow progress. No new API surface required.
pros: Zero additional API surface
Simple implementation
Works over any transport (REST, MCP, CLI)
cons: Latency between state changes and UI updates is bounded by polling interval
Frequent polling wastes resources when workflows are idle; infrequent polling misses rapid state changes
Cannot capture transient events (tool calls, LLM interactions) that complete between polls
Does not scale to concurrent workflow monitoring

options_considered.option: LangSmith traces as the observability layer
options_considered.summary: Use LangSmith's existing trace infrastructure for all observability. The CAS Application reads traces via the LangSmith API.
pros: Already available as part of the LangGraph selection (CAS-ADR-001)
Rich trace data including token usage, latency, and execution graphs
No additional ROOT Harness development
cons: Creates a dependency on an external service for a core CAS capability
LangSmith is a development and debugging tool, not a production event bus
Trace granularity and retention are controlled by LangSmith, not CAS
Does not emit CAS-specific semantic events (steward mutation proposals, governance decisions)
Would require the CAS Application to understand LangSmith's trace schema rather than a CAS-native event vocabulary

options_considered.option: Typed event stream on the Orchestration API
options_considered.summary: ROOT Harness emits a typed event stream during workflow execution. The CAS Application and MCP clients subscribe to the stream to observe execution in real time. Events use a CAS-specific taxonomy reflecting steward/orchestrator semantics, SAGE interactions, and governance decisions. The stream complements (does not replace) LangSmith traces for debugging and get_status for point-in-time queries.
pros: Real-time push eliminates polling latency
CAS-specific event taxonomy captures semantic events (mutation proposals, governance decisions, interrupt lifecycle) that generic trace tools cannot represent
Clean separation: the event stream is the observability interface; LangSmith remains the debugging tool; get_status remains the point-in-time query
Transport-adaptable: SSE for Phase 1 HTTP, WebSocket for Phase 2 if needed, stdio-compatible for MCP
Enables the CAS Application to build responsive UIs without understanding LangGraph internals
cons: New API surface to design, implement, and maintain
Event schema must be designed and specified in the formal substrate
Consumers must handle stream disconnection and reconnection

adrs.decision: ROOT Harness emits a typed event stream through the Orchestration API as the primary real-time observability mechanism for workflow execution. The event taxonomy is CAS-specific, reflecting the steward/orchestrator model, SAGE state interactions, mutation governance, and human-in-the-loop interrupt lifecycle. The stream is subscribed to via a new subscribe_events operation on the Orchestration API. LangSmith traces remain the debugging and diagnostic tool. The get_status operation remains the point-in-time query interface. The three mechanisms are complementary: subscribe_events for real-time observation, get_status for state queries, LangSmith for post-hoc debugging.
adrs.rationale: The CAS Application cannot fulfill its oversight role with polling alone. Transient events (tool calls completing, steward governance decisions, LLM interactions) are invisible to polling and essential for human monitoring. LangSmith provides rich traces but is an external development tool with its own schema, retention policies, and availability constraints; depending on it for production observability would violate the principle that core CAS capabilities should not depend on external services for their primary function. A CAS-native typed event stream gives the CAS Application exactly the semantic vocabulary it needs (steward mutations, orchestrator coordination, governance decisions) without requiring it to parse generic trace formats. The OpenHarness project's async-generator event pattern validated the approach: typed events yielded during execution, consumed by any presentation layer. CAS adapts the pattern to its own architectural vocabulary rather than adopting the OpenHarness taxonomy directly.
consequences: The Orchestration API gains a subscribe_events operation for real-time event stream subscription, filtered by workflow execution ID.

ROOT Harness defines a typed event taxonomy covering workflow lifecycle, LangGraph node transitions, agent tool interactions, LLM request/response cycles, interrupt lifecycle, steward governance events, and checkpoint operations.
The formal substrate gains an event schema specifying event types, required fields per type, and serialization format.
The CAS Application consumes the event stream as its primary mechanism for live workflow monitoring and agent activity display.
LangSmith traces and the get_status operation are preserved as complementary mechanisms for debugging and point-in-time queries respectively.
Transport selection for the event stream follows the phased deployment model: stdio-compatible for Phase 1 MCP, SSE or WebSocket for Phase 2 HTTP.

adrs.title: Named Core API operations replacing organize()
adrs.context: The SAGE Core API table (Section 7) defined organize(document_id, action, params) as a single operation covering lifecycle transitions (supersede, complete, archive, reactivate). ROOT Harness policy enforcement needs to gate operations at a granularity that matches its governance model. The policy schema's permitted_operations enum already used named operations (set_lifecycle, update_metadata) because ROOT Harness Section 4.3 and Section 3.5 reason in those terms. The Core API table was the outlier, bundling operations under organize() that the rest of the system already treated as distinct. With organize() as the API surface, every policy rule that needs to distinguish lifecycle transitions from metadata mutations must inspect the action parameter, pushing sub-operation parsing into the policy enforcement layer. This means ROOT Harness would be interpreting SAGE's internal dispatch semantics to enforce its own constraints, violating the boundary rule in spirit.

options_considered.option: Keep organize() and parse action parameter in policy enforcement
options_considered.summary: ROOT Harness policy layer inspects the action parameter of organize() calls to determine whether to allow, require approval, or deny.
pros: Fewer API operations (elegant, minimal surface)
No SAGE API change required
cons: Policy enforcement must understand SAGE's internal parameter semantics
Violates the boundary rule: ROOT Harness interprets SAGE dispatch logic
Brittle: adding a new organize() action requires coordinated policy updates
The formal substrate's policy schema already uses the named-operation grain, creating an impedance mismatch

options_considered.option: Decompose organize() into named operations
options_considered.summary: Replace organize() with set_lifecycle() for lifecycle transitions and update_metadata() for mutable metadata field mutations. Each operation is directly gatable by name.
pros: Policy rules are direct matches on operation names; no parameter inspection
Aligns the Core API with how ROOT Harness already reasons about operations
Each operation is simpler and self-documenting
The OpenAPI spec (v0.2) will be clearer with named endpoints
cons: More API surface (14 operations instead of 13)
Marginal loss of conceptual elegance from a single lifecycle-management entry point

options_considered.option: Add a separate archive() operation alongside organize()
options_considered.summary: Keep organize() for lifecycle transitions but split out archive() because it involves optional file-system moves.
pros: Addresses the archive-specific concern
cons: Half-measure: does not resolve the core policy-enforcement problem for other lifecycle transitions
Archive is a lifecycle transition in the state machine; special-casing it without splitting the others is inconsistent

adrs.decision: Decompose organize() into two named operations: set_lifecycle(document_id, action) for lifecycle transitions and update_metadata(document_id, fields) for mutable metadata field mutations. Archive is handled by set_lifecycle with action='archive'; it is a lifecycle transition in the state machine, and the optional file-system move is an internal SAGE implementation concern, not a distinct API operation.
adrs.rationale: The forcing function is policy enforcement. In an agentic system, behavioral constraints are a first-class architectural concern. The policy schema needs to gate at a granularity that matches the governance model. If organize() bundles lifecycle transitions and metadata updates under a single umbrella, policy enforcement must inspect parameters to distinguish them, which means ROOT Harness interprets SAGE's internal dispatch semantics. Named operations eliminate this: ROOT Harness gates on operation name alone. The practical test from the architecture prose confirms the grain: ROOT Harness Sections 3.5 and 4.3 already reason in terms of update_metadata and set_lifecycle as separate gatable actions. The formal substrate's policy schema enum reflected that natural grain from the start. The Core API table was the only place where the bundled organize() persisted.
consequences: The SAGE Core API table replaces organize(document_id, action, params) with set_lifecycle(document_id, action) and update_metadata(document_id, fields).
The formal substrate's policy schema permitted_operations enum no longer includes organize; it was already absent.
The SAGE Core API OpenAPI specification (deferred to formal substrate v0.2) will define set_lifecycle and update_metadata as separate endpoints.
Archive is a lifecycle transition (action='archive' on set_lifecycle), not a standalone operation.
PIM Health policy YAML files are updated to remove organize from permitted_operations lists.

adrs.title: Metadata extraction is a SAGE-level capability, not a caller responsibility
adrs.context: The vault_config schema (metadata_extraction.schema.json) declares a two-stage metadata extraction pipeline with explicit precedence: manual entry overrides content extraction overrides filename extraction. In practice this contract was partially unenforced. FilenameParser lived in app/backend/ and only the CAS Application's scan/ingest flow invoked it. The sage_ingest MCP tool called IngestionService.ingest without parsed metadata, so filename-derived fields (document_date, project, tags, version_label, doc_type) were left null and the source adapter's ProjectionResult.title (e.g., Word Title style or Markdown first H1) became the unconditional winner. The ingestion service then defaulted doc_type to 'misc' because no caller metadata supplied one. The symptom surfaced during Cowork session ingestion of a scaffolding-series docx: the Word Title style was extracted as the document title rather than the filename-derived catalog title, doc_type defaulted to 'misc', and project/tags/version_label were blank, requiring manual correction via sage_update_metadata. The root cause is architectural: the vault's declared metadata_extraction policy was enforced only when callers happened to parse filenames on their side. Different ingestion entry points (direct service call, MCP tool, app backend) produced different metadata from the same file.

options_considered.option: Require every caller to parse filenames before invoking sage_ingest
options_considered.summary: Keep FilenameParser in app/backend/. Update the sage_ingest MCP tool, CLI entrypoints, and any other caller to parse filenames and pass results as IngestRequest.metadata.
pros: Minimal code change inside SAGE itself
Preserves the current separation between catalog metadata (caller-supplied) and content metadata (adapter-extracted)
cons: Every ingestion entry point must re-implement the parse or import app.backend, inverting the SAGE-below-app layering
New entry points (agentic workflows, background ingest jobs) will forget to parse and reproduce the Cowork bug
The vault config declares a metadata extraction policy that is enforced inconsistently depending on caller discipline
Violates single-source-of-truth: the same parse logic must be invoked from multiple locations

options_considered.option: Move filename parsing into SAGE and invoke it uniformly during ingest
options_considered.summary: Relocate FilenameParser to sage/services/. IngestionService.ingest builds a parser from the vault's metadata_extraction config and invokes it on the source filename for every ingest. Parsed fields populate the document record per declared precedence: caller metadata > filename parse > adapter projection.
pros: Uniform behavior across all ingestion entry points (MCP tool, app backend, CLI, future agentic paths)
The vault's metadata_extraction policy is enforced wherever ingest runs
Eliminates the 'which caller parsed the filename' ambiguity
Aligns with the existing schema declaration that precedence is manual > content > filename
The review_required flag finally has end-to-end effect: SAGE marks metadata_confirmed at ingest based on the vault's trust declaration
cons: Modest refactor of IngestionService.ingest
App backend must update import paths (mechanical change)
Adapter's ProjectionResult.title becomes a content-extraction candidate rather than authoritative, a semantic shift (though not a contract break)

options_considered.option: Restructure adapters to return multiple title/metadata candidates
options_considered.summary: Redesign ProjectionResult to carry title_candidates and metadata_candidates dicts. IngestionService chooses winners per vault precedence.
pros: Most principled separation between extraction and reconciliation
Future adapters with multiple candidate sources (PDF with both XMP properties and a 'Title:' heading) compose cleanly
cons: Larger diff: every adapter touched
Not necessary to fix the Cowork bug; can be revisited later if genuine multi-candidate cases emerge
Overshoots the forcing function

adrs.decision: Relocate FilenameParser from app/backend/filename_parser.py to sage/services/filename_parser.py. IngestionService constructs a FilenameParser in __init__ when the vault declares a metadata_extraction.filename_extraction.pattern, and invokes it on every ingest. Parsed metadata populates the document record with precedence: caller-supplied IngestRequest.metadata > filename parse > adapter ProjectionResult.title. The default-to-'misc' doc_type fallback runs only when none of these sources yields a doc_type. IngestionService sets metadata_confirmed at ingest based on metadata_extraction.review_required.
adrs.rationale: Metadata extraction is a vault-level policy, not a per-caller concern. The vault config declares filename patterns, code-to-doc_type rules, and keyword rules; that declaration must be enforced wherever ingestion runs. Leaving extraction logic at the caller layer inverts the architecture: SAGE is the state substrate and owns the vault config, so SAGE is the natural home for extraction that consumes that config. The forcing function is uniform behavior across ingestion entry points. Adopting option 2 keeps the adapter contract minimal (ProjectionResult.title remains a single value; it simply loses precedence to a filename parse when the vault declares one) while moving the policy enforcement to the correct layer. The option-3 multi-candidate refactor addresses a larger generality that is not required to fix the observed failure and can be layered on later if a concrete adapter needs it.
consequences: FilenameParser moves from app/backend/ to sage/services/. The app backend imports it from its new location; behavior is unchanged.
IngestionService.ingest invokes FilenameParser on source_path.stem on every ingest when the vault has a filename_extraction pattern configured.

ProjectionResult.title is a content-extraction candidate: it loses to filename-parsed title when a vault pattern is configured, and wins when no pattern is configured (preserving behavior for vaults with ad-hoc naming).
The default-to-'misc' doc_type fallback fires only when filename parse, caller metadata, and existing record all fail to yield a doc_type.

metadata_extraction.review_required now controls metadata_confirmed at ingest: false (trusted conventions) marks documents confirmed automatically, true (review required) leaves documents unconfirmed for interactive confirmation via update_metadata.
SAGE Architecture Reference Section 3.4.6 (Metadata Extraction) updated to state that filename extraction is a SAGE-invoked stage, not a caller responsibility.

adrs.title: SAGE normalizes UI-layer file metadata on ingest
adrs.context: Agents routinely flag their working temp files invisible for their own hygiene. On macOS, this is done via the BSD UF_HIDDEN chflag and occasionally via the com.apple.FinderInfo extended attribute's invisible bit (0x40 in byte 8). When SAGE imports such a file into a vault, Python's shutil.copy2 propagates the UF_HIDDEN chflag to the destination (via os.chflags inside copystat). The destination is the canonical vault artifact, which then hides from Finder. An agent that subsequently deletes its temp file (correct hygiene: the vault now holds the canonical copy) leaves the user unable to see the canonical artifact in Finder at all. Observed in a Cowork session ingesting two Word documents: filenames did not begin with '.' and were not Word lock files, yet both the source temps and the vault copies were hidden. The vault is the state substrate; its files must remain user-auditable by definition. Propagating an agent's source-artifact UI intent to the canonical artifact is a category error.

options_considered.option: Do nothing; treat invisibility as a per-case remediation (chflags nohidden, xattr -d)
options_considered.summary: Accept that agents will occasionally leave canonical artifacts hidden; remediate when observed.
pros: Zero code change
Avoids silent metadata mutation on ingest
cons: Predictable failure mode, not a one-off: any agent that uses invisible temps will produce hidden canonical artifacts
The user is the one who finds out when auditing the vault and sees nothing
Forces the user to learn macOS xattr/chflags internals to recover visibility of their own state substrate

options_considered.option: Normalize UI-invisibility markers in SAGE on ingest
options_considered.summary: In IngestionService._ensure_vault_local, after shutil.copy2, clear the destination's UF_HIDDEN chflag and clear bit 0x40 in byte 8 of com.apple.FinderInfo (preserving other bytes). macOS-only; no-op elsewhere. Errors swallowed.
pros: Vault artifacts remain user-auditable by construction, independent of agent hygiene
Narrow and surgical: clears only the invisibility bits, not other Finder metadata (color labels, type codes, tags)
Platform-guarded: no effect on Linux or Windows ingestion
Zero dependency: uses stdlib os.chflags and ctypes for macOS xattr (no third-party package)
cons: Silent mutation of file metadata on copy -- surprising for anyone inspecting imports/ with xattr-aware tools
Adds a small macOS-specific code path to the ingestion pipeline

options_considered.option: Require callers to sanitize before invoking sage_ingest
options_considered.summary: Keep SAGE's copy path pure; expect callers (agents, app backend, CLI) to clear invisibility markers on their source files before ingest.
pros: Preserves strict copy semantics in SAGE
cons: Same caller-discipline antipattern that ADR-015 rejected: new entry points will forget and reproduce the bug
The vault's visibility contract would be enforced inconsistently depending on caller behavior
Agents would need macOS-specific sanitization logic in every caller

adrs.decision: IngestionService._ensure_vault_local invokes a sanitization helper _strip_ui_invisibility on every destination file copied from outside storage_root. The helper clears the BSD UF_HIDDEN chflag and clears bit 0x40 in byte 8 of com.apple.FinderInfo if present, preserving all other bytes of the xattr. The helper is a no-op on non-macOS platforms and when neither marker is present. Errors are swallowed: UI-layer sanitization is best-effort and must not fail an ingest.
adrs.rationale: The vault is the canonical state substrate; its artifacts are user-auditable by contract. UI-layer invisibility markers encode source-artifact semantics (an agent asserting 'this is my scratch, hide it from the user') and do not transfer to the canonical-artifact meaning ('the user will audit this'). Propagating them is a category error, not a preservation of user intent. The forcing function is the same boundary principle that motivates ADR-015: properties that SAGE's contract guarantees (visibility, extractable metadata, canonical identity) must be enforced at the SAGE layer, not delegated to caller discipline. The chosen sanitization is surgical -- it touches only the invisibility bits and leaves all other Finder metadata (color labels, type/creator codes, stationery flag) intact. This matters because color labels and tags are legitimate user-visible properties that should survive ingestion.
consequences: sage/services/ingestion.py gains a _strip_ui_invisibility helper that clears UF_HIDDEN and the com.apple.FinderInfo invisible bit on files copied into the vault's imports/ directory.
The helper uses ctypes to call libc's getxattr / setxattr / removexattr because Python stdlib has no xattr API on macOS. No new third-party dependency is added.
macOS Finder color labels, type codes, creator codes, and other FinderInfo fields are preserved through ingestion.
On Linux and Windows, the sanitization step is a no-op.

Generalizes: future UI-layer metadata mechanisms (quarantine flags, Spotlight tags, cloud-sync flags) are evaluated under the same principle. When a marker encodes source-artifact UI intent rather than canonical-artifact semantics, SAGE strips it on ingest.
